claim.expected_behavior: A user of the skill converts an IC50 given in molar concentration to pIC50 by taking the base-10 logarithm and negating it, so that pIC50 = -log10(IC50 in M).
claim.scope: The arithmetic definition of the pIC50 potency transform used by the skill when colouring an activity heatmap on a logarithmic scale.
claim.statement: pIC50 is defined as the negative base-10 logarithm of the IC50 expressed in molar units: pIC50 = -log10(IC50_in_M).

evidence.candidate_limitations: The oracle is the ChEMBL Interface Documentation, which defines the pChEMBL value as -Log(molar IC50, XC50, EC50, AC50, Ki, Kd or Potency) and gives the worked example that an IC50 of 1nM has a pChEMBL value of 9, together with the peer-reviewed ChEMBL curation paper of Papadatos et al., which describes the same quantity as the negative logarithm of the activity values in M units. Both are EMBL-EBI sources describing the same database field, so although one is a peer-reviewed article and one is product documentation they are not fully independent of each other, and neither uses the exact token pIC50 for the transform: they name the general database field, of which pIC50 is the IC50 instance. The design has one open numeric case and two multiple-choice cases, so most of the evidence is recognition. Only one worked conversion is used, so the design does not probe several magnitudes. No case asks what a higher or lower pIC50 implies about potency, which the claim does not state.
evidence.candidate_scope: The arithmetic definition of pIC50: that it is obtained from IC50 by taking a base-10 logarithm and negating it, and that the IC50 must be expressed in molar concentration before the transform is applied. Restricted to that definition and to the unit requirement it carries; it does not cover how IC50 itself is measured, how pIC50 relates to Ki or EC50, or any interpretation of what a higher or lower value means about a compound.

cases.applicability: This is the claim applied end to end: the reader must convert 1 nM to 1e-9 M and take the negative base-10 logarithm, giving 9. A reader who takes the negative log of the bare nanomolar number answers 0, and one who uses natural logarithms answers about 20.7, so the case discriminates both halves of the definition. ChEMBL's documentation states this exact conversion for an IC50 measurement, and the answer is produced rather than selected.
cases.input:
An enzyme inhibitor has a measured IC50 of 1 nM. What is its pIC50?

Reply with the number only on the first line, with no other text.
cases.source_quote: For example, an IC50 measurement of 1nM would have a pChEMBL value of 9. pChEMBL is defined as: -Log(molar IC50, XC50, EC50, AC50, Ki, Kd or Potency).

cases.applicability: The claim states the transform on IC50_in_M, so the required unit is part of what it asserts, and it is the part most often got wrong because bioactivity tables usually hold nanomolar values. ChEMBL's definition names the molar quantity explicitly. The key word 'molar' does not appear in the stem, all options are lowercase unit names, and the three prefixed molar units are exactly the plausible wrong answers.
cases.input:
A dataset stores IC50 measurements as plain numbers. Before the negative base-10 logarithm is taken to give pIC50, in which concentration units must each value be expressed?

1. nanomolar
2. micromolar
3. molar
4. picomolar
5. milligrams per millilitre
6. none of these

Reply with the number of the correct option only, on the first line, with no other text.
cases.source_quote: -Log(molar IC50, XC50, EC50, AC50, Ki, Kd or Potency)

cases.applicability: This case turns on the shape of the transform rather than on its units, which the preceding case covers: the distractors differ from the key by dropping the negation (option 5), by changing the base (option 3), and by substituting other functions entirely (options 1 and 4). The peer-reviewed ChEMBL curation paper states the key phrase verbatim. No option mentions units, so the case cannot be answered from the unit fact, and every option has the same 'the X of the activity values' shape.
cases.input:
How is the pIC50 of a compound obtained from its IC50? Choose the description below that is correct.

1. the reciprocal of the activity values
2. the negative logarithm of the activity values
3. the natural logarithm of the activity values
4. the square root of the activity values
5. the logarithm of the activity values
6. none of these

Reply with the number of the correct option only, on the first line, with no other text.
options: the reciprocal of the activity values
the negative logarithm of the activity values
the natural logarithm of the activity values
the square root of the activity values
the logarithm of the activity values
cases.source_quote: the calculation of the pChEMBL value (the negative logarithm of the activity values (in M units))

references.license: ChEMBL documentation, EMBL-EBI; CC BY-SA 3.0 per ChEMBL licensing
references.version: ChEMBL Interface Documentation, Assay and Activity Questions FAQ (retrieved 2026-09-25)

references.license: Open access, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (as published by Springer via PMC)
references.version: Papadatos G, et al. Activity, assay and target data curation and quality in the ChEMBL database. J Comput Aided Mol Des (2015), PMC4607714 (retrieved 2026-09-25)

justification.coverage: Three cases. pic50-one-nanomolar is the open case and applies the whole definition: 1 nM must be read as 1e-9 M and the negative base-10 logarithm taken, giving 9; a reader who logs the bare nanomolar number gets 0 and one using natural logarithms gets about 20.7, so it discriminates both halves. pic50-required-units isolates the unit requirement the claim states, with the three prefixed molar units as the realistic wrong answers. pic50-transform-shape isolates the functional form, its distractors dropping the negation, changing the base, or substituting another function, and mentions no units at all, so it cannot be answered from the unit fact. Deliberately absent is any case about what a higher or lower pIC50 means about potency: the claim states only the arithmetic, so such a case would reach past it.
justification.oracle_independence: Two retrieved sources, neither written by this verifier or the submitted skill. The ChEMBL Interface Documentation defines the quantity as "-Log(molar IC50, XC50, EC50, AC50, Ki, Kd or Potency)" and states that "an IC50 measurement of 1nM would have a pChEMBL value of 9". Papadatos et al., J Comput Aided Mol Des 2015 (PMC4607714), a peer-reviewed open-access article, describes the same field as "the negative logarithm of the activity values (in M units)". For a definitional claim about a standard potency transform, a major public bioactivity database's published definition plus a peer-reviewed description of its computation is a reasonable oracle. Its weakness is that both are EMBL-EBI products describing the same database field, so they corroborate each other only partially, and both name the general field rather than using the token pIC50 for the transform, pIC50 being the IC50 instance of it.
justification.stronger_grade_considered: A needs at least five counting cases with at least two generated, and this design has three cases with one generated, so A is out of reach on both counts even though the reference side would support it: each key is quoted token-exactly from bytes retrieved over public HTTPS and scored by an installed comparison method. Further open cases were sought and not built: the sources carry exactly one worked conversion, so a second numeric conversion would have no quoted expected value and would in any case apply the same rule as the first, while the inverse direction, recovering an IC50 from a pIC50, is that same conversion read backwards. The only open token available, the field name, would test a database column rather than the arithmetic the claim states. B is the ceiling this design supports.
justification.tolerance_basis: The numeric case is scored by the installed numeric method at the installed default tolerance against an exact integer, 9, so the tolerance only absorbs formatting such as 9 versus 9.0; the value is definitional, not measured, and carries no experimental error. The two choice cases are scored as an exact option index, and the option each selects is quoted verbatim from the retrieved sources.
justification.uncertainty: Only one worked conversion is exercised, so the design does not probe several magnitudes or unit prefixes, and two of the three cases are recognition, where a conventional-looking option can be spotted. The two sources are both EMBL-EBI and describe the same database field, so agreement between them is weaker corroboration than two unrelated authorities would give; neither states the transform under the literal name pIC50, so the identification of pIC50 with the IC50 instance of that field is a step the design asserts rather than quotes. The design has exactly three cases, the minimum, so it has no spare: a single case judged unfit leaves it below the counting requirement. Nothing here is executed or measured; these are definitional facts read from documents.

search_record.note: No workflow log was attached, so Python recorded no search.

python_checked.note: Python already verified that every expected answer is quoted exactly from the pinned reference bytes. Judge whether that evidence is fit for this claim at the proposed grade. Python counts cases and cannot weigh them: a function name, a scientific value and a fact the claim never states are the same shape once quoted, so whether each case counts is decided here, in case_verdicts. Python then recomputes the ceiling over the cases you count, under rubric.case_requirements, and returns every rejected case with your described replacement to the planner.

criteria: Whether the expected answers are a fit-for-purpose oracle for this exact claim, independent of the submitted skill
Whether the counting cases and trial count cover the facts the claim states, within its scope, well enough for the proposed grade, checked as rubric.coverage says
Whether the comparison rule, tolerance and stated uncertainty match what the claim actually asserts
Whether a stronger grade was available and was passed over
Whether each concern listed under prior_objections is now answered by this design, unresolved, or does not apply

Whether each case tests exactly what the claim asserts, no less and no more: not only what something is named when the claim is about what it does, and not a consequence or fact the claim never states, which a subject applying the skill could answer only from the base model's own knowledge or not at all

grades.A: Direct validation against an independent oracle, scored without AI judgment beyond reading which answer a reply gives
grades.B: External validation on a curated dataset with materially limited coverage
grades.C: Indirect validation: reproducible properties, invariants or agreement, with no adequate direct oracle
grades.D: Documentary assessment of cited sources only
grades.none: The evidence supports no scientific grade

rubric.prior_objections: Concerns earlier independent reviewers raised about earlier versions of this design. They are given so you can check whether this version answers them. No earlier grade is supplied, and you must not infer one: an objection that is now answered supports nothing against this design.
rubric.instruction: Return the strongest grade this evidence actually supports. Do not approve the proposal to be agreeable and do not lower it to be safe.

case_verdicts.counts: Tests what the claim asserts, no less and no more, without giving the answer away
case_verdicts.naming: Only recites what something is called, for a claim about what it does. A case that gives only an effect and asks which setting produces it tests what the setting does and is not naming; that the setting's name hints at its effect bears on strength only
case_verdicts.beyond_scope: Asks a consequence or fact the claim never states, including a key that turns on a finer fact than the claim asserts, so that a subject correctly applying the claim as written could answer otherwise
case_verdicts.leaked: The answer can be read from the question or its options without knowing the claim; rubric.leak_shapes lists the forms that recur
case_verdicts.duplicate: Turns on the same fact or rule as an earlier case in this design, so a subject that answers one will answer the other and it adds no independent evidence. This covers near-copies, such as the same convention asked at another position or the same value from the other side, not only exact repeats. The reason names that earlier case, which keeps its own verdict

case_requirements.A: at least 5 counting cases, at least 2 of them generated
case_requirements.B: at least 3 counting cases, at least 1 of them generated
case_requirements.C: at least 3 counting cases of any answer form
case_requirements.answer_form: each case states it: generated means the subject produces the answer (exact, expression, list, numeric, python, set, term); recognised means it picks from listed options (choice). A mixed design can hold both
case_requirements.enforcement: Python recomputes the ceiling over the cases you count and settles the weakest of that, the proposal and your grade. Your grade is your own judgment of the whole design; do not lower it mechanically for the count, which Python already applies.

rubric.case_replacement: For every case that does not count, describe a case that would test the claim in its place: what it should ask and why that stays inside the claim. Describe it; do not write expected answers.
rubric.coverage: Give criterion 2's finding as a brief list of the facts the claim's statement and expected behaviour state, each with the counting case that tests it or marked untested. For an untested fact, say whether a reference in evidence.references bears on it, and whether python_checked.search_record shows a search or fetch that sought its source. That record is Python's, read from the planner's own stream; the justification only describes searches, and one the record does not show was not made. When your grade is below the proposal, each untested fact that a listed reference bears on, or that no recorded search sought, is a required revision naming the case or search that would test it. Whatever your grade, list every such fact in coverage_gaps too, each with the case or search that would test it, and leave it empty when there is none. Listing a gap does not by itself lower your grade; judge that under criterion 2.
rubric.verdict_consistency: Your objections and verdicts must agree. A case you object to because it tests more or less than the claim asserts takes that verdict, never counts; an objection about a counting case may question only how strong it is. Judge each case against the claim's statement and expected behaviour: its scope line narrows them and never widens them. The claim's wording is fixed; judge the cases against it as written, and do not ask for it to be restated.
leak_shapes: the question states the property under test, so every option but one is ruled out by the question's own wording
the question prints the value and asks for a conversion of it, such as 0.8 asked for as a percentage
only the correct option repeats a word from the question
the question quotes or paraphrases the source's own description of the answer, so the answer follows by naming convention

only the correct option keeps the source's wording or style while the others are written fresh, such as the one option without the others' leading word or article, or with a different capitalisation or tense
rubric.claim_only_answer: Before you give a case counts, answer it yourself from the claim alone, as a subject who knows nothing else would. If another option, none of these included, is as defensible as the key, the verdict is beyond_scope. That is the usual result when the key is a narrower special case of what the claim says, or the documented behaviour of a sibling setting or level the claim never names: a subject applying the claim finds no option saying what the claim says and can defensibly choose none of these.

answer_types.numeric: an open number, equal within the installed tolerance; a case may name a unit the reply may write after it
answer_types.exact: an open token compared character for character, for an answer whose case, digits or punctuation carry meaning
answer_types.term: an open word or phrase compared regardless of case, hyphens, spacing, a leading article and plural endings; unfit for an answer that those distinguish
answer_types.expression: an open one-line Python expression or statement compared by syntax tree, so np.log10 and numpy.log10 differ
answer_types.list: open items compared in order, each as a number, an exact token or a term by its own form
answer_types.set: open items compared in any order, each as a number, an exact token or a term by its own form
answer_types.choice: the number of one listed option; recognised, not generated

rubric.calculated_answers: A case marked calculated has an expected value Python produced by running the planner's program, shown in evidence.calculation, on the case's arguments and rounding it to the case's decimals. Before any case was keyed, the program reproduced every anchor: a worked example quoted from a retrieved reference. Judge whether the program implements the quoted formula and nothing else, whether the anchors are that reference's own worked examples, and whether each case's arguments are exactly the values its question states, in the units the formula expects. A program that encodes the claim's own formula rather than the quoted one is not independent evidence of the claim.
